### Before you upgrade: every host has to be paired again, once

This release changes how a computer identifies itself. The host id used to be derived from the
machine's network interfaces, so plugging in a cable, toggling a VPN or switching Wi-Fi could
give the same computer a different identity — taking its pairings, its place in the host order
and its custom name with it. The id is now generated once and kept.

The cost is that **every host's id changes once on upgrade**. Remove each host on both computers
and add it again with the **same pairing password**. This is needed only once.

If you already installed any 0.1.11 beta, there is nothing further to do.

### The app is now called DisplayMuxAuto

The name matches the repository, and the project it extends is credited in the licence file,
both READMEs and the help page inside the app: this is an extension of
[DisplayMux](https://github.com/HenryHsu/DisplayMux) by Henry Hsu, under the MIT licence.

**Your settings are kept** — the identifier they are stored under deliberately stays as it was.
The installation itself differs by platform:

- **Windows**: the installer removes the old DisplayMux install and its autostart entry before
  installing.
- **macOS**: the updater replaces the app in place, so there is no second copy, but the file is
  still named `DisplayMux.app`. Rename it in Applications if you would like the two to agree.

### New

- **One display, more than one identity.** Some displays report a different identifier when they
  change display mode — 4K to 1080p, say — so the app read it as a different display and the
  sharing and port settings that belonged to it disappeared. You can now declare that the two are
  the same display; from then on they count as one, and the declaration is shared with paired
  hosts. A merge can be undone.
- **Reset**, in two scopes: displays only (paired hosts and the password are kept), or back to a
  fresh installation. The second keeps this computer's host identity, so there is nothing to
  clear on the other computer.
- **This computer can be named**, and the name reaches the switch centre, paired hosts and the
  name it is advertised under on the network. Leaving it empty restores the discovered machine
  name.
- **Ports can be set by hand.** Detection has a ceiling it cannot pass: a display reports the
  input it is showing, never which one the reader is plugged into, so a computer that has never
  been on screen cannot learn its own port. A port set by hand is shared with the other hosts
  exactly like a detected one.
- **Adding a host that is already set up fills in its port**, when the pairing verifies, both
  computers identify the same display, and that port is free. When it cannot be established
  safely, the choice is still yours.
- **The input list one host manages to read is shared with the others**, so a computer that
  cannot read that display still gets the right options.
- **The page says which settings wait for the save button.** Most of it saves as it is changed;
  the pairing password, the wait, autostart, update checks and the shortcut do not. Changing one
  of those five raises a note at the bottom, with a cancel beside it.

### Fixes

**Shared displays stop disappearing**

- A display that reports a different identifier after a display-mode change is no longer read as
  a different display, taking its settings with it.
- A display that cannot be read for a moment — because it is showing another host — is no longer
  dropped from sharing.
- A display removed from sharing, or cleared by a reset, is not selected back in.
- A display can be shared before it answers DDC/CI, and is read once it starts answering.

**Ports stop being guessed wrong**

- When a display's inputs cannot be read, no list of common ports is offered in their place. That
  list describes no particular display, and choosing from it can aim a switch at an input with
  nothing on it. The control says the inputs have not been read and keeps what is set.
- A detected value the display's own wiring contradicts is no longer stored.
- A guessed list no longer overwrites what another host actually read.

**Hosts keep each other current**

- After a rename, computers that have not paired yet see the new name in the search list too.
- A newly paired host receives what was already settled before it existed, instead of waiting for
  the next change.
- A notice that does not arrive is sent again on the next scan, until it lands.
- A paired host that moved is followed only once an authenticated connection confirms it.
- Both windows refresh themselves instead of showing whatever was true when you last acted.

**The global host switcher**

- **It had never worked on macOS.** The default shortcut was `Command+Option+Space`, which macOS
  binds to its Finder search window: registering it succeeds and the key never arrives. The
  default is now `Command/Ctrl+Shift+Space`, combinations the system reserves are refused when a
  shortcut is recorded, with the reason, and a saved one is replaced.
- After one successful switch the window stopped responding for good, reopening included.
- The host a display is already showing is no longer selectable, matching the dashboard.

**Messages and interface**

- A rejected request is no longer always reported as a wrong pairing password; a request the
  other host could not read because of a version gap says so.
- A rejected setting — a shortcut, a password, two hosts on one port — is no longer labelled
  "unable to complete the display operation", pointing at hardware that is fine.
- Each display's button shows its own progress, instead of reverting when a different display
  finishes.
- Reset shows that it is running.
- The icons on the display-identity cards and the unsaved-changes note draw instead of leaving
  empty squares.
- The sidebar no longer squashes the app icon out of shape.
- The reset warning reads as a warning rather than a disabled field.
- A paired host's row no longer breaks when more than one display is shared.

### Known limitations

- Undoing a merge leaves the inputs and notes that merging folded into the display the other
  identity joined.
- Ports, input lists, host names, input notes and merges only sync between hosts running this
  version.
- The macOS DMG is ad-hoc signed but not notarized with an Apple Developer ID, so Gatekeeper may
  require manual approval.
